operationalization: Define a representative inventory of deployed perceptual and analytical methods, then classify the structural regularities each can detect under standardized benchmarks. The claim is supported only if nearly all methods detect repetition or nesting but systematically fail on agreed higher-order structures.
obstacles: The quantifiers 'essentially all' and 'almost nothing more complex' lack fixed boundaries.
Method selection and the definition of higher-order regularity are contestable.
rationale: Existing benchmark results and method documentation could test restricted method classes. No comprehensive public census spans human perception and all practical mathematical, statistical, and computational analyses, and broad conclusions would depend heavily on taxonomy choices.

operationalization: Reanalyze public SETI recordings with prespecified searches for decodable, information-bearing structure beyond standard narrowband and transient detectors. A reproducible signal with non-natural encoding and independent recurrence would support the claim; null searches constrain only the searched encoding classes.

candidate_datasets.name: Breakthrough Listen Open Data Archive
candidate_datasets.role: public radio-telescope observations for alternative signal analyses

obstacles: Meaningfulness is not identifiable from arbitrary ciphertext-like noise without a key.
Available observations cover a tiny fraction of sources, times, frequencies, and signal types.
rationale: Large public radio datasets make many concrete searches possible now. The existential, open-ended wording and indistinguishability of sufficiently unfamiliar encoding from noise prevent a decisive resolution of the full claim.

operationalization: No non-arbitrary measurement can determine that computation is the single most important organizing idea; the input-output interpretation is a methodological convention.
obstacles: 'Most important' is evaluative rather than measurable.
The proposed framing has no unique empirical rival.
rationale: The claim recommends and ranks a conceptual framework. Applications can illustrate usefulness, but no dataset can confirm its asserted primacy without imposing the framework's own criteria.

operationalization: Viewing a system's state transition as a computation can be stipulated for any rule-governed evolution, but this supplies no observation that distinguishes the view from a non-computational description.
obstacles: The claim is primarily definitional.
No criterion for what would refute the computational description is supplied.
rationale: Specific systems can be given computational models, but the unrestricted statement is a representational choice. It has no measurable consequence distinct from redescribing state evolution.

operationalization: Choose explicit natural-system complexity tasks and compare predictive or explanatory performance of models that use computational universality with matched models that do not. Consistent, substantial gains would support usefulness for those tasks, not universal cruciality.
obstacles: 'Crucial' and 'understand' have no unique decision criteria.
Model comparisons would cover only selected natural systems.
rationale: Case studies can test whether universality-based analyses add value in defined domains. The broad methodological importance claim cannot be cleanly confirmed or refuted across natural science.

operationalization: Formalize universality as effective emulation of any machine in a standard universal model. The emulator construction directly establishes that the system can realize behaviors of arbitrary computable complexity; a failure of the universality premise would refute the implication's application.
obstacles: 'Complex' is informal unless identified with computational capability.
rationale: Under the standard meaning of computational universality, the conclusion follows directly from the definition and universal-machine theory. The qualification 'in a sense' matters, but the intended computational reading is explicit and checkable.

operationalization: Specify sampled classes of formal and natural systems, a physically justified computational model for each, and proof or emulation criteria for universality. Observing universality across preregistered representative samples would support prevalence within those classes.

candidate_datasets.name: Wolfram Atlas of Simple Programs
candidate_datasets.role: enumerated simple-system behaviors for restricted computational surveys

obstacles: There is no sampling frame over all computational or natural systems.
Natural-system universality depends on model and encoding assumptions.
rationale: Enumerated formal families and selected physical systems can be studied with existing resources. They cannot establish that universality is widespread over the claim's unrestricted domain or that abstract emulation is physically realized.

operationalization: Check the fixed 19-color automaton's encoding, local transition simulation, and iteration correspondence for an arbitrary target cellular automaton. A valid uniform construction proves the claim; a flaw or target rule outside the construction refutes it.
obstacles: Verification requires careful checking of a lengthy construction.
rationale: This is a precise universality theorem amenable to a finite, checkable simulation proof. Public descriptions and ordinary computation are sufficient to inspect representative instances and validate the general construction.

operationalization: For each listed formalism, verify a computable encoding into a universal cellular automaton and prove step or output equivalence. Standard computer architectures are covered by encoding finite logic, memory, and control into the universal simulation.
obstacles: 'Almost every type' is bounded only by the systems discussed in the book.
Practical emulation efficiency is not guaranteed.
rationale: Classical equivalence constructions among universal models settle the listed formal systems. The practical-computer phrase is also checkable in principle because finite digital hardware can be represented by circuits and memory.

operationalization: Compare represented configuration length after t steps under a fixed-radius cellular automaton with a substitution system having multiplicative length growth. A linear light-cone bound rules out a length-preserving one-CA-step-per-substitution-step spatial encoding of the stated kind.
obstacles: The impossibility depends on the intended local spatial encoding; highly compressed encodings require separate treatment.
rationale: The growth-rate argument is finite and mathematically checkable. It cleanly resolves the intended direct emulation, though an unrestricted notion of encoding would need sharper assumptions.

operationalization: Characterize words generated by independent symbol substitutions and prove their structural closure, then test whether a fixed local decoding can reproduce rule 30 spacetime behavior. Separately construct the direct neighbor-dependent substitution encoding of a cellular-automaton update.

candidate_datasets.name: Wolfram Atlas of Simple Programs
candidate_datasets.role: reference behavior for elementary cellular automata and substitution systems

obstacles: 'Nested' needs a formal language-theoretic definition.
Impossibility varies with the allowed encoding and time rescaling.
rationale: The constructive neighbor-dependent part is straightforward. The independent-substitution limitation is provable under a formalized direct-emulation notion, although the informal pattern vocabulary lowers operationalizability.

operationalization: Compose the simulator from a universal cellular automaton into each target formalism with the cellular automaton's simulations of arbitrary machines. Effective composition proves a universal member exists in every formalism with the assumed emulator.
rationale: This is a direct transitivity consequence of simulation and universality. Existing formal constructions can be checked without empirical data or large computation.

operationalization: Verify an encoding of register-machine configurations as integers and prove that each remainder-selected arithmetic update simulates the corresponding register instruction. Universality follows from the established universality of the simulated register-machine model.
obstacles: The exact allowed arithmetic rule family must be fixed.
rationale: The claim gives a constructive reduction between precise discrete systems. Its resolution requires checking the construction, not collecting new observations.

operationalization: Define equivalence as equality of computable functions up to effective encoding, then verify mutual simulations or universality for each listed formalism. A formalism unable to realize a computable function realized by another would refute equivalence.
obstacles: 'Fundamentally equivalent' is ambiguous outside computational expressiveness.
Efficiency and native dynamics are not preserved by universality.
rationale: For computational expressiveness, classical computability results settle the listed universal systems. The broader prose should not be read as equivalence in efficiency or structure, which the proof does not establish.

operationalization: Measure capability as the class of partial computable functions realizable under effective encodings. Prove that every universal system realizes that same class and that no ordinary algorithmic rule realizes more.
obstacles: The statement is false for resource efficiency, programmability, or physical capability unless capability is restricted to computability.
rationale: The saturation result is standard under extensional computability. Its informal 'nothing more' wording needs that qualification, but the intended context supplies it.

operationalization: Check the encoding of cyclic tag-system data and productions into rule 110 glider packages and verify that collisions implement each cyclic tag update. Since cyclic tag systems simulate universal Turing machines, a correct construction proves universality.

candidate_datasets.name: Cook, Universality in Elementary Cellular Automata
candidate_datasets.role: published checkable proof of rule 110 universality

obstacles: The construction is intricate but finite and checkable.
rationale: A published constructive proof directly settles this precise theorem. The proof and rule are public, and representative transitions can be independently simulated with modest resources.

operationalization: Predefine system families, a rule-description complexity measure, and universality criteria, then estimate the fraction of universal members by proof or bounded emulation searches. High fractions across multiple low-complexity families would support the restricted prevalence claim.

candidate_datasets.name: Wolfram Atlas of Simple Programs
candidate_datasets.role: survey resource for simple rule families and observed behaviors

obstacles: Universality is generally undecidable.
There is no canonical measure or sampling distribution over 'systems of all kinds'.
rationale: Existing enumerations permit informative surveys in finite rule spaces. They cannot resolve the extrapolation to a very wide range of all simple systems, and non-discovery of proofs does not establish nonuniversality.

operationalization: For specified enumerated rule families and complexity metrics, compute long-run behavioral statistics as description length increases and locate proven universal members. Early plateaus across preregistered metrics would support saturation within those families.

candidate_datasets.name: Wolfram Atlas of Simple Programs
candidate_datasets.role: existing enumerations and visualizations of simple-program behavior

obstacles: Behavioral complexity has many inequivalent metrics.
Finite simulations cannot establish asymptotic behavior or universality.
Results from selected rule orderings need not generalize across system types.
rationale: The finite survey component is reproducible from public rules and software. The universal statement and causal identification of a low universality threshold remain underdetermined.

operationalization: Formalize class 4 by asymptotic dynamical criteria and prove that every cellular automaton satisfying them can simulate a universal machine, or exhibit a rigorously class-4 nonuniversal counterexample.

candidate_datasets.name: Wolfram Atlas of Simple Programs
candidate_datasets.role: candidate cellular automata for restricted searches

obstacles: Class 4 lacks a single rigorous definition.
Universality is undecidable in broad cellular-automaton classes.
No finite simulation can confirm the universal quantifier.
rationale: Existing examples can support searches but do not settle the implication. Resolution requires a new general theorem or counterexample and a precise class-4 definition.

operationalization: Exhaustively simulate all 256 elementary rules over a prespecified suite of initial conditions and apply explicit class-4 criteria, quotienting by reflection and color complementation. Repeat on bounded multicolor and larger-neighborhood families to estimate class-4 frequency.

candidate_datasets.name: Wolfram Atlas of Simple Programs
candidate_datasets.role: complete elementary cellular-automaton rule catalog and behavior examples

obstacles: 'Clear immediate example' is observer- and horizon-dependent.
The multicolor and larger-neighborhood scope is unbounded.
rationale: The elementary-rule census is complete and easy to rerun. Classification ambiguity and the open-ended comparative claim prevent full resolution, though explicit proxies can strongly test it.

operationalization: Give rigorous dynamical definitions of class 1 and class 2 with bounded information propagation, then prove that their bounded communication or eventual periodicity cannot implement arbitrarily large universal computations.

candidate_datasets.name: Wolfram Atlas of Simple Programs
candidate_datasets.role: reference catalog for class-1 and class-2 cellular automata

obstacles: Wolfram classes are phenomenological rather than uniquely formal.
Some formal definitions of class 2 may not imply a uniform propagation bound.
rationale: Under the bounded-information interpretation stated in the claim, a clean impossibility proof is available. Ambiguity in assigning all cellular automata to phenomenological classes slightly weakens full-scope certainty.

operationalization: For additive rules, derive the linear superposition and power-of-two recurrence over the finite field, then prove this constrained evolution cannot realize an arbitrary nonlinear cellular automaton under the intended encoding. Treat formally defined nested-pattern rules by an analogous structural invariant.

candidate_datasets.name: Wolfram Atlas of Simple Programs
candidate_datasets.role: rule 90 and rule 150 behavior and definitions

obstacles: The broad category 'nested-pattern' needs formal definition.
Impossibility depends on permitted encodings.
rationale: Linear cellular automata have exact algebraic descriptions that support strong nonuniversality results. The additive examples are directly resolvable; the wider informal nested category is less sharply bounded.

operationalization: Reconstruct the stated enumeration order, evolve rule 54 from each of the first 100 million finite initial conditions to a prespecified horizon, and classify each trace using explicit periodicity and nesting tests. One certified counterexample refutes the observation; exhaustive agreement confirms it only for the chosen horizon and definitions.

candidate_datasets.name: Wolfram Atlas of Simple Programs
candidate_datasets.role: public rule definition and reference behavior for rule 54

obstacles: The simulation horizon is not stated.
Fundamental complexity and nesting require operational definitions.
rationale: The finite rule and initial-condition range can be regenerated with standard computation. Some interpretation is required, but the bounded historical observation is reproducible rather than a claim about all time.

operationalization: Define non-repetitive and non-nested behavior formally, then prove universality for every system satisfying the definition or construct a qualifying nonuniversal counterexample.

candidate_datasets.name: Wolfram Atlas of Simple Programs
candidate_datasets.role: candidate-system catalog for counterexample searches

obstacles: The behavioral categories are informal.
The scope over all systems is not enumerable under one formalism.
Universality is undecidable in general.
rationale: Current finite surveys can test selected families but cannot resolve the unrestricted implication. A new theorem or decisive counterexample is needed after substantial formalization.

operationalization: Measure damage spreading from single-cell perturbations and compare the availability of persistent localized structures and proof constructions across classified rules. A strong association between spreading and failed component-based constructions would support this particular methodological mechanism.

candidate_datasets.name: Wolfram Atlas of Simple Programs
candidate_datasets.role: cellular-automaton rules and behaviors for damage-spreading analyses

obstacles: Proof difficulty is partly sociological and method-dependent.
Failure to find components does not imply none exist.
Not every class 3 rule has identical perturbation dynamics.
rationale: Damage spreading and localized structures are computable for finite samples. Existing analyses cannot cleanly establish that uncontrolled flow causes proof difficulty in general or excludes other proof methods.

operationalization: Construct a computable encoding and simulation of a known universal machine in each of rules 30 and 45, or prove an invariant that makes such simulation impossible. Simulations can search for components but cannot by themselves establish universality.

candidate_datasets.name: Wolfram Atlas of Simple Programs
candidate_datasets.role: rule 30 and rule 45 definitions and observed behaviors

obstacles: No accepted universality proof is available for these rules.
Universality cannot be confirmed by bounded runs.
Class-3 information spreading obstructs known construction methods.
rationale: The claim is precise enough once universality is standardly defined, but public simulations do not settle it. New mathematical constructions or impossibility results are required.

operationalization: Enumerate block sizes and encodings for each underlying rule and verify whether one encoded update reproduces each of the 256 elementary target-rule truth tables. The finite list of successful target rules directly confirms or refutes the stated contrast.

candidate_datasets.name: Wolfram Atlas of Simple Programs
candidate_datasets.role: complete definitions and reference behavior for all 256 elementary rules

obstacles: The allowed block encodings and maximum searched block size must match the claim.
A failed bounded search does not prove impossibility.
rationale: Positive single-step emulations are finite certificates that are easy to verify. Claims that simple rules emulate only a few require either a proven bound or careful restriction to the reported search.

operationalization: For each symmetry-identified elementary rule counted among the 27 candidates, provide a universality proof or a nonuniversality proof and count the universal rules. The numerical prediction is supported if the final count accords with the stated upper estimate.

candidate_datasets.name: Wolfram Atlas of Simple Programs
candidate_datasets.role: complete elementary-rule catalog and candidate behaviors

obstacles: Most candidate rules lack universality or nonuniversality proofs.
Finite behavioral complexity does not establish universality.
The phrase 'perhaps as many as' is a weak decision target.
rationale: The finite domain is fully known, but the decisive property is not computably settled by ordinary enumeration. Substantial new proofs are needed for many rules.

operationalization: Check the 2-state 5-symbol transition table and prove that one complete sweep implements one encoded rule 110 step while preserving delimiters and state. Composing this with rule 110 universality proves the machine universal.

candidate_datasets.name: Cook, Universality in Elementary Cellular Automata
candidate_datasets.role: establishes universality of the simulated rule 110 system

obstacles: The exact transition table and encoding construction must be checked.
rationale: This is a finite constructive reduction to an established universal system. It is independently verifiable by proof and simulation with standard resources.

operationalization: Enumerate all 4096 transition tables modulo relevant symmetries, derive each machine's possible tape dynamics for arbitrary finite input, and prove every case enters a restricted nonuniversal behavior class.
obstacles: Blank-tape simulation alone would not rule out universality on encoded inputs.
The Turing-machine convention must be fixed.
rationale: The machine space is finite and small, and a case-reduced mathematical analysis can settle arbitrary-input capability. Merely observing simple blank-tape traces would be insufficient, but stronger existing methods make the claim resolvable.

operationalization: Enumerate all machines in the stated finite spaces under the book's numbering and blank-tape convention, run each to a declared horizon, quotient by specified symmetries, and classify complexity with prespecified recurrence and growth metrics.
obstacles: 'Complex behavior' is not uniquely defined.
Counts can depend on runtime cutoff and equivalence conventions.
rationale: All transition tables can be regenerated exactly, so no external empirical data are missing. Reproduction is straightforward after matching conventions, though the qualitative complexity threshold introduces interpretation.

operationalization: Provide a universal-machine simulation encoded in machine 596,440 or prove an invariant excluding universality, then compare its state-symbol size under a fixed minimality measure with all smaller machines.
obstacles: Complex blank-tape behavior is not evidence sufficient for universality.
A universality proof or obstruction is missing.
'Simplest' varies across machine-size measures and conventions.
rationale: The target machine is finite and fully specified, but bounded computation cannot settle universality. The secondary minimality claim also requires exhaustive nonuniversality results for smaller machine classes.

operationalization: Enumerate all 2,985,984 machines from blank tape, simulate to a prespecified horizon, and detect halting, periodic, and nested traces. For nonblank inputs, sample or symbolically analyze explicit input classes and search for traces that fail to simplify.
obstacles: No finite horizon proves eventual simplicity.
The set of complicated initial conditions is unbounded.
Repetitive and nested need formal classifiers.
rationale: The blank-tape finite census is directly reproducible and strongly testable. Existing finite runs cannot resolve the claim over all more complicated inputs or all future times.

operationalization: Reduce the stated length-8 S-K expression while measuring term size and structural statistics, and verify a formal encoding of rule 110 in combinator reduction. Exponential growth and the emulation construction test the concrete claims, while perceived randomness requires chosen statistics.

candidate_datasets.name: Cook, Universality in Elementary Cellular Automata
candidate_datasets.role: universal source system for checking the claimed combinator emulation

obstacles: 'Highly complex' and 'seemingly random' are metric-dependent.
Naive combinator reduction can cause severe expression growth.
rationale: Combinator rules and initial expressions are exact and publicly reproducible, and universality is already established independently. Standard symbolic software can test the concrete growth and emulation components.

operationalization: One can map state transitions in any chosen rule-governed process to an input-output computation, but no observation distinguishes this optional representation from another exact description.
obstacles: The claim proposes a conceptual framework.
The unrestricted quantifier and 'viewed as' provide no falsification criterion.
rationale: Examples can demonstrate that the framing is possible and useful, but cannot empirically establish a universal interpretive convention. The statement is not a distinct prediction about process behavior.

operationalization: Define obvious simplicity, a sampling distribution over a bounded formal system family, and sophistication as computational universality, then estimate the universal fraction using proofs and certified simulations. Repeating this across families tests restricted versions.

candidate_datasets.name: Wolfram Atlas of Simple Programs
candidate_datasets.role: existing survey of behavior across several simple-program families

obstacles: There is no canonical measure over all processes.
Universality is undecidable in general.
Natural processes cannot be exhaustively sampled or assigned exact rules.
rationale: Finite formal families permit partial empirical and mathematical tests. Existing resources cannot resolve 'almost all' across nature, mathematics, and engineered systems or establish a unique maximal sophistication notion.

operationalization: Specify hypercomputation models and identify their required physical resources, then compare those requirements with tested physical laws and bounds. A reproducible physical device computing a formally non-Turing-computable function would refute the claim; existing physics can exclude particular proposals.
obstacles: No finite set of observations covers every constructible system in the universe.
The inference depends on extrapolating physical laws to untested regimes.
Hypercomputation cannot be certified from finitely many input-output trials alone.
rationale: Existing theory and experiments can reject specific hypercomputer designs based on infinite precision, energy, or time. They cannot decisively prove the unrestricted physical Church-Turing thesis.

operationalization: For each precisely defined rule family and size distribution, classify obvious simplicity and prove or disprove universality for the remaining rules, then calculate the asymptotic universal fraction.

candidate_datasets.name: Wolfram Atlas of Simple Programs
candidate_datasets.role: behavioral catalog for restricted simple-program families

obstacles: No canonical distribution exists over all possible rules.
Universality is undecidable in broad families.
Behavioral non-simplicity does not itself certify universality.
rationale: Available enumerations allow bounded estimates but leave many members unclassified. The asserted overwhelming fraction and cross-family scope require major new mathematical results and explicit measures.

operationalization: Choose natural domains with inferred mechanistic rules, quantify rule-description complexity and evidence of selection constraints, and compare their distribution with a prespecified random-rule ensemble. Then test computational universality for the matched models where possible.
obstacles: Nature supplies no unbiased sampling frame of governing rules.
Inferred rules depend on model choice and observational scale.
Random selection requires an arbitrary measure over rule descriptions.
rationale: Selected physical and biological model collections could test a narrow version. Existing data cannot establish that most unconstrained natural rules are effectively random or almost always universal.

operationalization: For every finite binary word, prove that some row of the single-seed rule 30 spacetime diagram contains it, or find a finite word and prove it never occurs. Enumeration can confirm occurrence only up to finite block length.

candidate_datasets.name: Wolfram Atlas of Simple Programs
candidate_datasets.role: rule 30 definition and existing computed spacetime patterns

obstacles: Finite simulation cannot establish the all-blocks quantifier.
No known general occurrence proof or forbidden-block proof settles the claim.
The computation-directory interpretation is stronger than block occurrence alone.
rationale: The property is mathematically precise and arbitrarily large finite searches are easy. Existing results do not resolve the infinite quantifier, so a new theorem or counterexample is needed.

operationalization: For preregistered classes of large molecules and glasses, compare experimentally observed structures with independently calculated global minimum-energy structures and characterized metastable basins. A predominance of demonstrably metastable observed states supports the restricted claim.

candidate_datasets.name: RCSB Protein Data Bank
candidate_datasets.role: public experimentally determined macromolecular structures

obstacles: Global energy minima are computationally difficult to establish.
Observed structures depend on solvent, temperature, kinetics, and measurement conditions.
Public structures are biased toward tractable molecules and do not cover glasses broadly.
rationale: Many observed molecular structures and energy models exist, enabling tests in selected domains. Coverage and reliable global-minimum identification are insufficient for the broad statement about complicated molecules generally.

operationalization: Specify physically reasonable continuity, noise, precision, and resource assumptions, then prove that each continuous evolution can be simulated to required observable accuracy by a Turing machine. Explicit continuous models computing nonrecursive functions under those assumptions would refute it.
obstacles: Different analog-computation models have different power.
The result depends critically on computable parameters, finite precision, robustness, and resource bounds.
Ideal mathematical continuity is not itself experimentally testable.
rationale: Computable-analysis theorems resolve substantial model classes, and physical precision limits constrain real analog devices. The claim's inclusion of idealized continuous systems under unspecified 'reasonable assumptions' prevents a single complete test.

operationalization: Check a reduction mapping an arbitrary infinite cellular-automaton evolution or halting instance to existence of a solution of an equation using integers, arithmetic, and trigonometric functions. Correct equivalence proves undecidability; a flaw in the encoding refutes the construction.
obstacles: The statement depends on the exact equation language, domain, and meaning of 'finding a solution'.
The contrast with pure polynomial equations changes when integer rather than real solutions are allowed.
rationale: Undecidability reductions for equations with periodic functions are finite mathematical objects and can be checked now. Careful domain restrictions are essential, but no new empirical observations are needed.

operationalization: Define a target set of cognitive mechanisms and a quantitative simplicity measure, then fit mechanistic computational models to open neural and behavioral datasets and compare them with more complex rivals on held-out interventions and predictions.

candidate_datasets.name: Human Connectome Project
candidate_datasets.role: public multimodal human brain and behavioral measurements

obstacles: 'Basic mechanisms' and 'rather simple' lack fixed criteria.
Observational equivalence permits many computational models of the same behavior.
Current neural datasets have limited resolution and intervention coverage.
rationale: Existing neuroscience data can evaluate specific simple mechanistic accounts. They cannot identify all mechanisms of thought or establish the broad computational ceiling as stated.

operationalization: For explicitly sampled simple-program families, search for algebraic invariants, compression, prediction shortcuts, and universality proofs beyond repetition and nesting. Discovery of a broad exploitable invariant would refute a restricted version; repeated failure would not prove absence.

candidate_datasets.name: Wolfram Atlas of Simple Programs
candidate_datasets.role: existing behaviors across simple-program families for regularity searches

obstacles: Absence of hidden regularity is not finitely verifiable.
A 'large class' and 'hidden regularity' have no unique definitions.
Universality does not imply absence of all useful regularities.
rationale: Public enumerations permit meaningful searches and counterexamples in chosen families. No feasible analysis can confirm the universal negative or infer computational equivalence merely from failure to detect structure.

operationalization: For specified systems and observer algorithms, establish computational equivalence formally and measure prediction, compression, and classification performance. Compare with weaker observers to test whether matched computational power predicts perceived complexity in those cases.

candidate_datasets.name: Wolfram Atlas of Simple Programs
candidate_datasets.role: simple-system behavior for restricted observer-performance experiments

obstacles: Perceived complexity is observer- and task-dependent.
Computational equivalence does not by itself imply equal practical prediction difficulty.
The quantifier over every usable perception and analysis method is open-ended.
rationale: Restricted observer-system pairs can be studied with existing simulations and proofs. The proposed universal causal explanation is too broad and underspecified to discriminate cleanly from alternatives such as resource bounds or poor representations.
